course.description: The Joy of Learning reading menu for EDCOR 310: talks, essays, podcasts, and debates beyond the textbook, about an hour a week.

intro.lede: The Joy of Learning readings are where you get to follow a question, meet a compelling idea, or explore a debate beyond the course textbook.

sections.head: The requirement.
sections.body: Each week, spend about one hour with readings from the current unit's menu: articles, talks, podcasts, videos, essays, and more.

sections.head: Choose your path.
sections.body: Pick the readings that genuinely interest you. The times are rough stopping points, not always the full runtime. When a reading says “~20 min,” spend about 20 minutes with it and then move on. If you want to keep going, see extra credit below.

sections.head: Use the jigsaw.
sections.body: Divide the options among your group so each person studies something different, then teach your reading back to the group. The goal is to keep overlap low and get the most learning for the whole group.

sections.head: Learn actively.
sections.body: As you read or listen, find the author's main claim, the evidence or reasoning behind it, and one point that surprised, challenged, or interested you. Be ready to explain the material in your own words.

sections.head: Make it useful.
sections.body: In your prep checks, explain what you read and show your notes. If you read extra for extra credit, provide slides that cover all of your sources (not just the first hour) and a short video recording explaining what you read and what you learned. Name your favorite ideas, explain how they will change you, and connect the material to educational psychology, teaching, human development, or your own life.

sections.head: Keep an open mind.
sections.body: Some readings are compelling, intriguing, controversial, or even divisive. You do not have to agree with everything you read. Your job is to understand the argument fairly, evaluate it thoughtfully, and add something worthwhile to the conversation.

sections.head: Extra credit.
sections.body: One hour is required. Each extra hour of real engagement earns extra credit worth half as much as the hour before: 2 hours → 15/10, 3 hours → 17.5/10, and so on, up to a maximum of 20/10.

sections.head: AI and the other readings.
sections.body: The Joy of Learning readings are separate from the Applied Readings and the course textbook. You may use AI to clarify a difficult idea after you have engaged with the material yourself, but your group should hear your understanding of the reading, not an AI-generated substitute for it.

sections.head: Using this page.
sections.body: Press “I’ll read this” to track your minutes against the unit’s requirement, and “My group has it” for readings a groupmate has claimed. Your picks are saved in this browser only. “Copy my list” gives you your readings and links to paste wherever you need them.

units.label: Unit 1
units.title: Introduction to Psychology
units.blurb: Where educational psychology begins: what education is for, why human judgment needs help, how evidence improves professional practice, why science has limits, and what it might mean to build a life and classroom that flourish.

entries.title: Coddling vs. Strengthening University
entries.hook: Should education protect students from difficulty?
entries.blurb: Jonathan Haidt argues that students become stronger when education exposes them to challenge, disagreement, and the possibility of being wrong. A lively opening argument about what college is supposed to do and what kind of person learning should form.
entries.source: YouTube — watch about 30 minutes.

entries.title: Rethinking Fast and Slow: The Importance of Intuition
entries.hook: Is intuition always the enemy of good thinking?
entries.blurb: Carl Hendrick revisits the relationship between fast and slow thinking and asks when intuition reflects expertise rather than bias. A useful counterweight to the simple story that careful reasoning is good and intuition is bad.
entries.source: Carl Hendrick on Substack — read for up to 20 minutes.

entries.title: What Really Works in Teaching and Learning
entries.hook: What does effective teaching actually look like?
entries.blurb: Carl Hendrick surveys the research behind explicit instruction, teacher talk, motivation, assessment, professional development, and the role of AI in education. A wide-ranging, practical conversation about turning research into better classroom practice, and about telling genuinely useful ideas from fashionable ones.
entries.source: The EduDisruptor Podcast with Carl Hendrick — listen for up to 60 minutes.

entries.title: The Holy Art of Skepticism (lecture)
entries.hook: Skepticism is not cynicism.
entries.blurb: In his William James Lecture in Psychology, Benjamin Pacini (your instructor) treats skepticism as an intellectual virtue: a disciplined willingness to ask what we know, how we know it, and what would change our minds. This is the big, slow-thinking option.
entries.source: William James Lecture in Psychology (2024) — watch about 60 minutes.

entries.title: The Holy Art of Skepticism (essay series)
entries.hook: Rather read than watch?
entries.blurb: The written version of the same argument, in a series of essays by Benjamin Pacini. Start with Part I and keep going through the series. Choose this or the lecture, not both.
entries.source: Benjamin Pacini on Substack — read until you reach about 60 minutes.

entries.title: The Oedipus Trap
entries.hook: What happens when a theory becomes impossible to escape?
entries.blurb: A case study in how compelling stories can become self-confirming explanations. The Oedipus story gives you a memorable way to think about bias, professional judgment, and the danger of interpreting every outcome as proof that the theory was right.
entries.source: EconTalk with Megan McArdle — listen for about 30 minutes.

entries.title: Why Do School Psychs Cling to Ineffective Practices?
entries.hook: Why do trained professionals hold on to weak ideas?
entries.blurb: This short piece asks why evidence does not automatically dislodge familiar practices. It is a direct invitation to think about professional responsibility, institutional incentives, and what it means to practice education well.
entries.source: School Psyched Podcast (about 68 minutes) — listen for 15 minutes.

entries.title: Visible Learning, Part 1: Disasters and Below-Average Methods
entries.hook: What does it mean to say that something works?
entries.blurb: John Hattie walks through teaching methods whose average effects are weak, or worse. Listen for how he compares effects across studies, and ask whether a small difference would matter in a real classroom.
entries.source: John Hattie talk — watch the whole thing. Watch Part 1 before Part 2.

entries.title: Visible Learning, Part 2: Effective Methods
entries.hook: Which methods clear the bar, and how high is the bar?
entries.blurb: The second half of Hattie's talk turns to methods with stronger average effects. Pay attention to the yardstick he uses to call something effective, and to what an effect size can and can't tell a teacher.
entries.source: John Hattie talk — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: Sold a Story: The Problem
entries.hook: How does an educational idea become common before it is well tested?
entries.blurb: This episode follows the consequences of a widely adopted approach to reading instruction. It is a compelling case study of the research-to-practice gap and of how good intentions, institutional momentum, and persuasive stories can outrun evidence.
entries.source: American Public Media — listen to Episode 1 for about 30 minutes.

entries.title: The Replication Crisis
entries.hook: What should we do when science gets something wrong?
entries.blurb: A story about failed replications, scientific self-correction, and the uncomfortable distance between a published finding and a dependable truth. The goal is not to lose faith in science, but to understand why good science needs humility, repetition, and revision.
entries.source: You Are Not So Smart — listen for about 30 minutes.

entries.title: The Rise and Fall of Peer Review
entries.hook: Who watches the watchers of science?
entries.blurb: Adam Mastroianni examines peer review as a necessary but imperfect institution. This is a chance to think about how knowledge is filtered, how quality control can fail, and why the imperfections of science do not make every claim equally credible.
entries.source: Adam Mastroianni — read for about 30 minutes.

entries.title: Social Psychology Won't Save Us
entries.hook: Can a scientific explanation solve a human problem by itself?
entries.blurb: This conversation pushes against overconfident applications of social psychology. It asks you to distinguish a useful scientific finding from the temptation to treat one study, one effect, or one framework as a complete answer to a human question.
entries.source: Art of Manliness — listen for about 30 minutes.

entries.title: #fakescience
entries.hook: Why does bad science spread so easily?
entries.blurb: A public-facing story about scientific fraud, hype, incentives, and the conditions that reward confident claims. It offers a concrete way to explore why the scientific method matters and why institutions still need wise judgment.
entries.source: The Weeds — listen for about 30 minutes.

entries.title: The Scandal That Shook Psychology to Its Core
entries.hook: What happens when a field's most famous findings fail to replicate?
entries.blurb: This short video introduces a scandal in psychology and the larger questions it raises about replication, publication incentives, statistical practices, and scientific self-correction. Use it to distinguish a flawed study from a flawed scientific enterprise.
entries.source: Neuro Transmissions (the video runs about 30 minutes) — stop around 10.

entries.title: Is Most Published Research Wrong?
entries.hook: Is the published literature more certain than the evidence beneath it?
entries.blurb: This short video asks why published research can look more definitive than the underlying evidence. Bring back one way that publication practices, incentives, or selective reporting can shape what gets noticed.
entries.source: Veritasium — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: Are Most Papers Never Cited?
entries.hook: What does it mean if much of the research we publish is rarely used?
entries.blurb: This short article examines how often academic papers are cited, read, or forgotten. Ask whether citation counts measure importance, visibility, usefulness, or merely attention, and what that means for how we evaluate knowledge.
entries.source: LSE Impact Blog — read the whole article.

entries.title: The Great Rewiring
entries.hook: What happens when childhood moves onto the phone?
entries.blurb: Jonathan Haidt connects technology, development, and the mental-health crisis facing young people. The piece invites you to consider how environments shape attention, relationships, and flourishing, and how difficult it is to separate a compelling argument from a settled conclusion.
entries.source: Jonathan Haidt — watch the first 20 minutes.

entries.title: The Surprising Science of Happiness
entries.hook: Are you good at predicting what will make you happy?
entries.blurb: Daniel Gilbert uses research on happiness to unsettle our intuitions about the future. It is an accessible, memorable lesson in how people misjudge what they will want, what they will feel, and what experiences will matter.
entries.source: TED talk — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: How to Make Stress Your Friend
entries.hook: Can the meaning we give stress change what stress does?
entries.blurb: Kelly McGonigal presents a provocative argument about stress and interpretation. Treat it as an opportunity to evaluate a popular claim carefully: what is promising, what is supported, and where might a helpful idea be overgeneralized?
entries.source: TED talk — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: Living After the Manner of Happiness
entries.hook: What does a good life ask of us?
entries.blurb: Jeffrey R. Holland offers a values-rich account of happiness, responsibility, and human flourishing. Read it in conversation with the psychological accounts in this unit and ask what a scientific description can illuminate, and what it cannot decide for us.
entries.source: BYU-Idaho Speeches — listen for about 35 minutes.

entries.title: Positive Psychology: An Overview
entries.hook: What would it mean to study what helps people flourish?
entries.blurb: A short introduction to positive psychology: the study of strengths, well-being, and the conditions of a good life.
entries.source: Society for Personality and Social Psychology — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: What Is Positive Psychology?
entries.hook: Is flourishing more than feeling good?
entries.blurb: A quick explainer on what positive psychology studies and why it doesn't reduce happiness to a single feeling. A good warm-up for Seligman's talk.
entries.source: Short video — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: Martin Seligman: The New Era of Positive Psychology
entries.hook: What if psychology studied what goes right?
entries.blurb: Martin Seligman, a founder of positive psychology, argues that psychology should study strengths and well-being, not only illness. It gives you a research-based vocabulary for talking about the good life.
entries.source: TED talk — watch the whole thing.

units.label: Unit 2
units.title: Developmental Psychology
units.blurb: What shapes a person? Unit 2 moves from the early environment of parenting and play through sex, gender, adolescence, morality, mindset, personality, and agency. These readings ask not only what develops, but how much our choices and circumstances can change us.

entries.title: Does Parenting Matter?
entries.hook: If parenting shapes children, how much does it shape them?
entries.blurb: The Intelligence Squared debate puts competing interpretations of behavioral-genetic and developmental evidence into direct conversation. Listen for what each side means by matter, what counts as evidence, and where a useful conclusion might be more modest than either opening position.
entries.source: Intelligence Squared debate — listen for about 45 minutes.

entries.title: The One Parenting Decision That Really Matters
entries.hook: If most parenting advice is lower-impact than it sounds, what decision might matter most?
entries.blurb: A compact Atlantic argument about one high-leverage parenting choice. Read it alongside the parenting debate and ask whether the evidence supports a universal rule, a narrower claim, or a useful question for parents and teachers.
entries.source: The Atlantic (PDF) — read the whole article.

entries.title: Two Parent Privilege
entries.hook: If family structure is associated with child outcomes, how should we talk about it without turning correlation into blame?
entries.blurb: Melissa Kearney makes a data-centered case for the advantages associated with two-parent households and for the social consequences of family structure. It is a useful, uncomfortable counterpoint to the claim that parenting matters little.
entries.source: Melissa Kearney — watch about 30 minutes.

entries.title: Peter Gray: The Decline of Play
entries.hook: What do children lose when play is crowded out?
entries.blurb: Psychologist Peter Gray connects the decline of free play to rising anxiety and depression in children, and makes the case for protecting time that kids run themselves. Bring back his strongest argument and the strongest objection.
entries.source: TEDxNavesink — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: Peter Gray: How Our Schools Thwart Passions
entries.hook: Can school get in the way of curiosity?
entries.blurb: Peter Gray argues that standard schooling can crowd out the self-directed exploration where lasting interests grow. Ask what a teacher could do inside a school to leave room for it.
entries.source: TEDxAsburyPark — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: Sir Ken Robinson: Do Schools Kill Creativity?
entries.hook: Does school teach creativity out of children?
entries.blurb: One of the most-watched TED talks ever: a funny, pointed case that schools rank some kinds of intelligence above others and teach children to fear mistakes. Enjoy it, then ask which claims are argued and which are backed by evidence.
entries.source: TED talk — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: Monkeys and Morality: Crash Course Psychology #19
entries.hook: What does a baby monkey want more: food or comfort?
entries.blurb: Crash Course covers Harlow's attachment studies and early moral development. Use it to ask what kinds of early experiences build security and self-regulation.
entries.source: Crash Course — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: Watching SpongeBob Makes Preschoolers Slower Thinkers, Study Finds
entries.hook: Can nine minutes of a fast cartoon change how a four-year-old thinks?
entries.blurb: A news write-up of a small experiment on fast-paced TV and preschoolers' self-control. Read it twice: once for the finding, and once for what a single short study can and can't show.
entries.source: ABC News — read the whole article.

entries.title: How Pretend Play Can Help Kids Socially and Emotionally
entries.hook: What does make-believe teach?
entries.blurb: A local news segment on dramatic play and its social and emotional benefits for young children. Ask which claims sound like evidence and which sound like hope.
entries.source: WMAR-2 News — watch the whole thing.

weeks.title: Week 6
notes: Some Week 6 readings address sexuality, gender, and religious identity directly. Read generously and critically; the assignment is to understand and teach an argument accurately before evaluating it.

entries.title: The Case for Heroic Masculinity
entries.hook: What might masculinity be for?
entries.blurb: A Public Square essay argues for a form of masculinity organized around courage, sacrifice, responsibility, and service. Read it as a claim about ideals rather than as a description of every man, then ask which parts are psychological, cultural, moral, or theological.
entries.source: Public Square Magazine — read the whole piece.

entries.title: Why “All In” LGBT+ and SSA Saints Are So Reluctant to Speak Up
entries.hook: Why might people who feel included still hesitate to speak?
entries.blurb: This piece asks how identity, religious belonging, social risk, and public conflict interact. Bring one insight about creating a classroom where difficult questions can be discussed without requiring students to hide or perform an approved identity.
entries.source: Public Square Magazine — read the whole piece.

entries.title: Sexuality and Gender: Executive Summary
entries.hook: What did a much-debated 2016 report actually claim?
entries.blurb: The executive summary of Lawrence Mayer and Paul McHugh's report in The New Atlantis, which reviewed research on sexual orientation and gender identity. Read the claims carefully before you read the criticism.
entries.source: The New Atlantis — read the whole summary.

entries.title: Profs. Criticized for “Anti-LGBT” Paper
entries.hook: How did colleagues respond?
entries.blurb: The Johns Hopkins student newspaper reports the criticism the report drew from faculty. The goal is not to pick a team quickly. It is to understand the argument, the criticism, the rhetoric, and how hard it is to discuss contested research responsibly.
entries.source: Johns Hopkins News-Letter — read the whole article.

entries.title: Richard Reeves: Male Inequality, Explained
entries.hook: What does gender inequality look like when we examine men's lives?
entries.blurb: Richard Reeves lays out where boys and men are falling behind in school, work, and family life, and what might help.
entries.source: Big Think — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: Let Us Be Men
entries.hook: What does a good man look like?
entries.blurb: Elder D. Todd Christofferson's general conference talk calls men to integrity, responsibility, and service. Read it alongside Reeves and notice the different registers: social analysis there, religious exhortation here.
entries.source: General conference, October 2006 — read the whole talk.

entries.title: Disney “Princess Culture” May Make Children More Progressive About Women
entries.hook: How do stories teach children what men and women are supposed to be?
entries.blurb: A news story on a BYU study of princess culture and children's later attitudes. Notice where the article reports evidence and where it interprets it.
entries.source: Salt Lake Tribune — read the whole article.

entries.title: In Praise of the New Femininity
entries.hook: What might femininity be for?
entries.blurb: A Deseret News perspective piece on femininity and masculinity. Notice where it describes evidence, where it makes value judgments, and where the two kinds of claim get blended.
entries.source: Deseret News — read the whole piece.

entries.title: The Two Trees
entries.hook: What does the story of Eden say about men, women, and partnership?
entries.blurb: Valerie Hudson Cassler reads the Garden of Eden as an account of two complementary gifts, from Eve and from Adam, and draws out what it might mean for marriage and partnership.
entries.source: FAIR Conference, 2010 — read for about 30 minutes.

entries.title: Designed for Covenant Relationships
entries.hook: What are we designed for?
entries.blurb: Jenet Jacob Erickson, a family scholar, argues that human beings are built for committed, covenant relationships, drawing on both research and Latter-day Saint teaching.
entries.source: BYU Speeches (2022) — watch for about 30 minutes.

entries.title: Designed for Love and Connection. Designed for Family.
entries.hook: What does it mean to be made for love and connection?
entries.blurb: In a BYU-Idaho devotional, Jenet Jacob Erickson makes the case that people are designed for love, connection, and family, and asks what that means for how we live.
entries.source: BYU-Idaho devotional, February 2025 — read the whole talk.

entries.title: It Takes Two
entries.hook: Do children need both a mother and a father?
entries.blurb: Subtitled “What We Learn from Social Science about the Divine Pattern of Gender Complementarity in Parenting.” It reads research on mothers and fathers alongside the doctrine of the family.
entries.source: PDF — read for about 30 minutes.

weeks.title: Week 7
notes: The Witch Trials contains violence, school-shooting references, and profanity. If that material is not a good fit for you, choose another Week 7 reading and let me know if you need an alternative.

entries.title: Why the Mental Health of Liberal Girls Sank First and Fastest
entries.hook: Why did some teens decline faster than others?
entries.blurb: Jonathan Haidt asks why the decline in teen mental health hit liberal girls hardest. Bring back the strongest evidence and the strongest caveat you can find.
entries.source: After Babel — read for about 20 minutes.

entries.title: The Case for Phone-Free Schools
entries.hook: Should phones be locked away for the whole school day?
entries.blurb: Jonathan Haidt argues that schools should go phone-free from the first bell to the last, and answers the common objections.
entries.source: After Babel — read for about 20 minutes.

entries.title: Yes, We Do Know Social Media Isn't Safe for Kids
entries.hook: Is the evidence too weak to act on?
entries.blurb: Psychologist Jean Twenge answers critics who say the research on social media and teen mental health is too uncertain to justify action.
entries.source: After Babel — read the whole piece.

entries.title: Social Media Is a Major Cause of the Mental Illness Epidemic in Teen Girls. Here's the Evidence.
entries.hook: How strong is the evidence that social media harms teen girls?
entries.blurb: Jonathan Haidt lays out the evidence he finds most convincing: correlational, longitudinal, and experimental. Read it the way a skeptic would.
entries.source: After Babel — read for about 20 minutes.

entries.title: Discerning the Impact of Influencers
entries.hook: What makes an influence trustworthy?
entries.blurb: Amanda Freebairn offers eight questions for weighing whether an influencer's content points people toward Christ, without condemning every influencer who raises concerns.
entries.source: Public Square Magazine — read the whole piece.

entries.title: Saying Goodbye to Faith-Toxic Influencers
entries.hook: When should you hit unfollow?
entries.blurb: Dan Ellsworth compares following faith-critical influencers to an emotional affair and urges readers to choose carefully whom they follow. Ask what makes an influence manipulative, and how adolescents learn to tell the difference.
entries.source: Public Square Magazine — read the whole piece.

entries.title: The World Is Awful. The World Is Much Better. The World Can Be Much Better.
entries.hook: Can all three be true at once?
entries.blurb: Max Roser of Our World in Data argues that the world is still terrible in many ways, has improved enormously, and can improve much more. A model for seeing danger without losing proportion.
entries.source: Our World in Data — read the whole piece.

entries.title: Don't Teach Your Kids to Fear the World
entries.hook: What happens when children learn to see threats everywhere?
entries.blurb: An op-ed from the American Enterprise Institute argues that teaching children to fear the world does them harm. Consider the developmental cost of both exaggerated optimism and exaggerated threat.
entries.source: AEI — read the whole piece.

entries.title: Moral Intuitions and Persuasion
entries.hook: Why do moral arguments so often begin with a feeling and end with a justification?
entries.blurb: This talk gives you a way to think about moral intuition, persuasion, and disagreement. Listen for the difference between understanding the psychological source of a judgment and deciding whether the judgment is right.
entries.source: FAIR Conference, 2022 — watch or read for about 25 minutes.

entries.title: The Righteous Mind: Summary and Takeaways
entries.hook: What do people do when they know what they think but can't explain why?
entries.blurb: A summary of Jonathan Haidt's book The Righteous Mind, including moral dumbfounding: being sure something is wrong without being able to say why.
entries.source: Marble Jar Channel — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: Jonathan Haidt: Is Morality Real?
entries.hook: Where do our moral judgments come from?
entries.blurb: Jonathan Haidt talks with Tim Ferriss about moral intuition and the foundations of moral judgment.
entries.source: The Tim Ferriss Show (clip) — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: Moral Foundations Theory
entries.hook: What are the moral foundations?
entries.blurb: A short explainer on moral foundations theory: the idea that moral judgment draws on several distinct intuitions, such as care, fairness, loyalty, authority, and sanctity. Treat it as a compelling theory, then ask what evidence would support it, challenge it, or show that it works differently across cultures.
entries.source: IDRlabs — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: The Witch Trials of J.K. Rowling
entries.hook: What does courage look like when a public disagreement becomes a moral crisis?
entries.blurb: Choose one episode of The Witch Trials of J.K. Rowling and teach your group what it reveals about moral conviction, social pressure, and the stories people tell about disagreement. Episodes 1 and 2 are the gentlest entry point; later episodes are more intense.
entries.source: Podcast — listen to one episode for about 30 minutes.

entries.title: You Are Safe in My Classroom
entries.hook: What should safety, truth, and belonging mean in a classroom?
entries.blurb: A Public Square piece about truth, belonging, and pride flags asks teachers to navigate care, identity, institutional expectations, and disagreement. Bring one principle you think belongs in every classroom and one tension that principle does not resolve.
entries.source: Public Square Magazine — read the whole piece.

units.label: Unit 3
units.title: Motivational Psychology
units.blurb: By what are we motivated? Unit 3 is about what moves us: personality, culture, community, and finally, agency. These readings ask whether we choose to move or whether our biology moves us. They also build a foundation for a future teacher's work in managing classroom behavior and sculpting souls: character development and effective classroom culture.

entries.title: The Moral Obligation of Self Worth
entries.hook: Treat yourself like someone you are responsible for helping.
entries.blurb: Jordan Peterson explains why we often fail to care for ourselves properly, and why responsible self-respect may be the beginning of genuine self-care and growth.
entries.source: Jordan Peterson — watch the video.

entries.title: Becoming More in Christ: The Parable of the Slope
entries.hook: Where we start is not the same thing as where we are headed.
entries.blurb: Elder Clark G. Gilbert uses the metaphor of a mathematical slope to explore growth, unequal starting points, grace, high expectations, and our divine potential in Christ.
entries.source: General conference, October 2021 — read the whole talk.

entries.title: Why Modern America Creates Fragile Children
entries.hook: What if protection sometimes prevents the development it is meant to secure?
entries.blurb: This provocative argument examines the unintended consequences of overprotection. Consider when efforts to keep children safe may prevent them from developing independence, confidence, and resilience.
entries.source: Big Think — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: What Personality Predicts Better Teachers?
entries.hook: What actually predicts effective teaching?
entries.blurb: This short piece challenges our intuitive assumptions about what makes a great teacher. Consider what personality research can, and cannot, tell us about teaching effectiveness.
entries.source: The Skeptical Educator — read the whole piece.

entries.title: How to Be More Resilient
entries.hook: Resilience is not merely a trait; it is also a set of practices.
entries.blurb: Use this practical introduction to identify one strategy you could teach to a student, or practice yourself, when facing stress, failure, or discouragement.
entries.source: Therapy in a Nutshell — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: The Success Paradox
entries.hook: Can the pursuit of success quietly change what we want?
entries.blurb: Success can motivate us, but it can also change what we notice, want, and value. Consider whether achievement is producing genuine flourishing, or simply moving the finish line farther away.
entries.source: Veritasium — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: His Grace Is Sufficient
entries.hook: How can people believe they are becoming more when they still see so much they need to change?
entries.blurb: Brad Wilcox offers a memorable account of grace, effort, and gradual development. Read it alongside the psychology of mindset and ask where the metaphor illuminates learning and where it makes a claim psychology cannot test.
entries.source: BYU Speeches — read the whole talk.

entries.title: The Super Mario Effect
entries.hook: Can a game change how failure feels?
entries.blurb: Mark Rober uses a familiar game to explain persistence, feedback, and the way goals can make repeated failure tolerable. Translate the idea into a classroom and ask what would have to be true for the analogy to work.
entries.source: Mark Rober at TEDx — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: Activism Versus Discipleship
entries.hook: When does moral commitment strengthen a person, and when can it blind one?
entries.blurb: Brother Ahmad Corbitt distinguishes activism from discipleship and warns that righteous language can still produce distorted judgment. Choose the video or transcript and consider how the argument applies to identity, agency, and moral development.
entries.source: Video — watch about 20 minutes, or read the transcript.

entries.title: Personality Is Bogus
entries.hook: What does a personality test actually measure?
entries.blurb: Crash Course makes the provocative case that personality categories can mislead. Use it as a starting point for distinguishing popular labels, trait measurement, prediction, and the possibility that people behave differently in different situations.
entries.source: Crash Course Psychology — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: Daniel Dennett: Stop Telling People They Don't Have Free Will
entries.hook: How much of what you do is chosen, and how much is caused?
entries.blurb: Philosopher Daniel Dennett explains why he thinks telling people they lack free will is both mistaken and harmful.
entries.source: Big Think — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: Elder Bednar: There Is No Free Agency, Only Moral Agency
entries.hook: Why does the word agency matter?
entries.blurb: Elder David A. Bednar explains why he speaks of moral agency rather than free agency, and what that difference means for responsibility.
entries.source: Short video — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: Being an Agent to Act
entries.hook: What does it mean to act rather than be acted upon?
entries.blurb: Elder David A. Bednar teaches that we are agents to act, not objects to be acted upon, and what that asks of a learner.
entries.source: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: Do Personality Tests Work?
entries.hook: Why do personality tests feel so revealing?
entries.blurb: TED-Ed traces the history of the Myers-Briggs and asks whether popular personality tests measure anything that predicts behavior.
entries.source: TED-Ed — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: The Big Five Personality Traits
entries.hook: Which personality model has the strongest evidence?
entries.blurb: A short animated explainer of the Big Five: openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, and neuroticism.
entries.source: Sprouts — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: Is There Science Behind the Five Love Languages?
entries.hook: Do love languages hold up?
entries.blurb: Greater Good looks at what research says about the popular five love languages. A good test case for a framework that may entertain more than it predicts.
entries.source: Greater Good Magazine — read the whole article.

entries.title: Trait Theory: Big Five vs. HEXACO
entries.hook: What does a sixth trait add?
entries.blurb: A comparison of the Big Five with the HEXACO model, which adds honesty-humility. Bring back one useful distinction between a test that entertains, a test that describes, and a test that predicts.
entries.source: Short lecture — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: Body Ritual Among the Nacirema
entries.hook: What looks strange when we study another culture may look perfectly normal from inside our own.
entries.blurb: This memorable anthropology exercise makes the familiar feel foreign. Describe the Nacirema culture accurately, then use the discomfort to ask how cultural distance, language, and professional vocabulary shape what we think we are observing.
entries.source: Horace Miner's article (PDF) — read the whole thing.

entries.title: Dead Poets Society: “Rip It Out”
entries.hook: Who decides what a poem is worth?
entries.blurb: Mr. Keating has his students tear the introduction out of their poetry textbook. Watch for authority, norms, and how a group responds when a teacher breaks the rules.
entries.source: Film clip — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: Dead Poets Society: Conformity
entries.hook: Why do we fall into step?
entries.blurb: Keating has three students walk in the courtyard, and their steps quickly sync up. A small study in how conformity happens without anyone asking for it.
entries.source: Film clip — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: Dead Poets Society: “O Captain! My Captain!”
entries.hook: When does a group create courage?
entries.blurb: The film's final scene, as students decide whether to stand on their desks. Bring back one moment in which the group creates courage and one in which it creates conformity.
entries.source: Film clip — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: The Moral Roots of Liberals and Conservatives
entries.hook: Why can good people look at the same moral question and see entirely different worlds?
entries.blurb: Jonathan Haidt's classic talk introduces moral foundations and shows how liberals and conservatives weigh them differently. Treat it as a compelling framework, not a final verdict.
entries.source: TED talk — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: Jonathan Haidt: The Moral Foundations of the Left and Right
entries.hook: Can understanding the other side's morality make disagreement kinder?
entries.blurb: A short clip from Jonathan Haidt's conversation with John Anderson about moral foundations and political conflict. Ask what the framework explains well and what it risks flattening.
entries.source: John Anderson interview (clip) — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: Jonathan Haidt: The Righteous Mind
entries.hook: How deep do our political divisions go?
entries.blurb: A two-minute clip of Jonathan Haidt on the central idea of The Righteous Mind: moral intuitions bind people into teams. Ask how it might help people disagree with more charity.
entries.source: Grand Valley State University (clip) — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: Expressive Individualism and the Restored Gospel
entries.hook: What happens when the self becomes the highest authority on who we are?
entries.blurb: Jeffrey Thayne contrasts expressive individualism, which puts self-expression at the center of the good life, with a restored-gospel worldview centered on covenants and becoming like God.
entries.source: Public Square Magazine — read the whole piece.

entries.title: Worldview Apologetics: Revealing the Waters in Which We Swim
entries.hook: What assumptions do we carry without noticing?
entries.blurb: A FAIR Conference talk on how culture hands us invisible assumptions about identity, freedom, truth, and fulfillment, and how to bring them into view.
entries.source: FAIR Conference, 2021 — read for about 25 minutes.

entries.title: The Bobo Beatdown: Crash Course Psychology #12
entries.hook: How much of what we learn comes from watching someone else?
entries.blurb: Crash Course covers Bandura's Bobo doll experiment and learning through observation and modeling.
entries.source: Crash Course — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: Vygotsky's Theory of Cognitive Development
entries.hook: What can a learner do with a little help?
entries.blurb: A short animated explainer of Vygotsky: language, scaffolding, and the zone of proximal development. Compare it with Bandura's route into social learning.
entries.source: Sprouts — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: Moral Grandstanding
entries.hook: What happens when moral language becomes a way to display virtue in public?
entries.blurb: This short talk introduces moral grandstanding, online signaling, and the incentives that can turn moral concern into status competition. Bring one example of moral grandstanding and one reason to be cautious about the concept.
entries.source: Big Think — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: Audience Capture
entries.hook: Can an audience gradually train a creator to say more of what the audience rewards?
entries.blurb: Use this short video to think about social media, reinforcement, identity, and the way public approval can narrow a person's judgment. Bring back one example of audience capture from online life or public discourse.
entries.source: After Skool — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: I Can Tolerate Anything Except the Outgroup
entries.hook: Why are we often most charitable toward people we already agree with?
entries.blurb: Scott Alexander uses forgiveness, tolerance, political tribes, and filter bubbles to examine how outgroups are formed and why our compassion can become selective. Read critically: the essay is provocative and includes political and religious content.
entries.source: Slate Star Codex — read for about 30 minutes.

weeks.title: Week 10
notes: The Jon Ronson piece describes online harassment and calls for violence. Durkheim's piece concerns suicide. Choose another Week 10 reading if either topic is not a good fit for you.

entries.title: The Overjustification Effect
entries.hook: Can a reward make someone less interested in the thing they were already enjoying?
entries.blurb: This short video introduces the idea that external rewards can sometimes crowd out intrinsic motivation. Translate the claim into a classroom example, then ask when rewards clarify expectations, when they support practice, and when they backfire.
entries.source: Game Maker's Toolkit — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: Motivation as Drive Reduction
entries.hook: Can motivation be explained as the reduction of biological tension?
entries.blurb: This primer introduces drive-reduction theory as one attempt to explain behavior, then gives you a way to compare it with incentives, intrinsic motivation, and other accounts of why people act.
entries.source: Crash Course Psychology — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: How One Tweet Can Ruin Your Life
entries.hook: What happens when a mistake becomes a public identity?
entries.blurb: Jon Ronson tells a story about online outrage, shame, and social punishment. The piece is useful for thinking about behavior change, proportionality, reputation, and the difference between accountability that repairs and condemnation that consumes.
entries.source: Jon Ronson at TED — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: Durkheim on Suicide
entries.hook: What if a deeply personal act is partly shaped by the strength of a person's social bonds?
entries.blurb: Durkheim's classic argument treats social integration and regulation as central to understanding suicide. Focus on the sociological idea rather than trying to master every detail, and be ready to explain what an individual-level account might miss.
entries.source: The School of Life — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: The Great Behaviorism Manifesto
entries.hook: What if behaviorism is more powerful, more humane, and more misunderstood than people think?
entries.blurb: Benjamin Pacini makes the strongest case he can for behaviorism as a practical science of changing environments and behavior. You do not need to agree with the manifesto; you do need to identify its best argument and the point at which you resist it.
entries.source: Benjamin Pacini on Substack — read for about 30 minutes.

entries.title: In Praise of Shame
entries.hook: Can shame ever be a force for good?
entries.blurb: This essay offers a deliberately provocative argument about shame, conscience, and moral formation. Read it as an argument to test: distinguish useful moral discomfort from humiliation, and ask what kind of shame helps a person return rather than retreat.
entries.source: Benjamin Pacini on Substack — read Part I.

units.label: Unit 4
units.title: Cognitive Psychology
units.blurb: How does the brain learn? Unit 4 is true educational psychology: memory, learning, attention, and how to change minds that want to stay stubborn. These readings are essential for anyone engaged in the business of soulcraft, beginning with how to capture attention and ending with protecting yourself from the pressures of the school you will end up in.

entries.title: ADHD: Inhibition, Impulsivity, and Emotion
entries.hook: What looks like a lack of effort may be a problem of inhibition.
entries.blurb: From Russell Barkley's “30 Essential Ideas” series: how ADHD affects inhibition, impulse control, and emotion. Bring back one misconception it corrects.
entries.source: Russell Barkley lecture — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: How to Treat ADHD Based on Science
entries.hook: What does evidence-based ADHD treatment look like?
entries.blurb: Russell Barkley walks through the treatments with the strongest research behind them. Bring back one question the talk leaves open.
entries.source: Russell Barkley, 2012 Burnett Lecture — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: What Is the Difference Between ADHD and Executive Function Deficits?
entries.hook: Are ADHD and executive-function problems the same thing?
entries.blurb: A short clinic article on how ADHD relates to executive-function deficits, and how the two differ.
entries.source: Article — read the whole thing.

entries.title: ADHD and the Lack of Play Opportunity
entries.hook: What happens when a developmental explanation becomes a public argument?
entries.blurb: Russell Barkley responds to Jordan Peterson's claims about ADHD and play. Listen for how experts define evidence, how disagreements become personal, and how a good rebuttal can correct a claim without pretending the underlying question is simple.
entries.source: Russell Barkley — watch about 30 minutes.

entries.title: Why It's So Hard to Achieve a Goal
entries.hook: Why do goals stall?
entries.blurb: How to ADHD and coach Alan Graham on why goals fall apart and how to set ones that get done. Translate one idea into a classroom support that builds independence rather than simply removing the task.
entries.source: How to ADHD — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: What Is Executive Function and Why Do We Need It?
entries.hook: What is executive function?
entries.blurb: A plain explainer on the brain's management system: planning, working memory, self-control, and flexible thinking.
entries.source: How to ADHD — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: Types of Memory: Short-Term, Working, and Long-Term
entries.hook: Which memory system is doing the work?
entries.blurb: A clear tour of the types of memory. Connect working memory to what a student who struggles with executive function faces in class.
entries.source: JJ Medicine — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: How to Homework: Top 10 Tips for ADHD Success
entries.hook: Why is homework so hard to start?
entries.blurb: Practical strategies for doing homework with ADHD. Sort them into supports that change the task, the environment, or the learner.
entries.source: How to ADHD — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: ADHD and Motivation
entries.hook: Why can't you just make yourself do it?
entries.blurb: Why motivation works differently for people with ADHD, and which supports make action easier without turning support into surrender.
entries.source: How to ADHD — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: How Dopamine Affects Learning and Motivation in ADHD Brains
entries.hook: What does dopamine have to do with getting started?
entries.blurb: An explainer on dopamine, reward, and why interest matters so much for people with ADHD. Watch for which claims are well supported and which are simplified.
entries.source: How to ADHD — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: How Exercise Can Help with ADHD
entries.hook: Can moving help you focus?
entries.blurb: What exercise does for attention and mood, and practical ways to build it into a day.
entries.source: How to ADHD — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: 5 Ways People Try to Help Someone with ADHD That Aren't Helpful
entries.hook: When does help backfire?
entries.blurb: Five common kinds of “help” that don't help, and what to do instead. Ask which might turn a complex problem into a character judgment.
entries.source: How to ADHD — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: The Student Engagement Trap
entries.hook: What if students can look engaged while learning very little?
entries.blurb: This Edutopia piece distinguishes enjoyable activity from genuine learning. Use it to connect executive function, cognitive effort, and classroom design, then bring one example of an engagement strategy that might be serving the wrong master.
entries.source: Edutopia — read the whole article.

entries.title: Best Five Strategies for ADHD
entries.hook: What supports are most useful when attention, planning, and inhibition are hard?
entries.blurb: Use this practical set to distinguish strategies that change the environment from strategies that simply ask a student to try harder. Bring back one strategy and one limitation or unanswered question.
entries.source: How to ADHD — watch the whole thing.

weeks.title: Week 12
notes: The James Flynn talk includes a reference to sexualized violence. Choose another intelligence reading if you prefer to avoid that content.

entries.title: Belonging at Church
entries.hook: What does it take for a community to feel like yours?
entries.blurb: Benjamin Pacini (your instructor) argues that belonging grows less from friendliness tactics than from members working together toward shared spiritual goals. Look for the difference between being present, being welcomed, being needed, and being known.
entries.source: Public Square Magazine — read the whole piece.

entries.title: And Not One Soul Shall Feel Excluded
entries.hook: Is inclusion the same as validation?
entries.blurb: Dan Ellsworth argues that inclusion is part of Christian discipleship but has to be guided by doctrine and virtue, and that responsibility for belonging is shared.
entries.source: Public Square Magazine — read the whole piece.

entries.title: Stand Fast with Love in Proclaiming Truth
entries.hook: How can a community hold truth and love together when people feel threatened by both?
entries.blurb: President Dallin H. Oaks and Elder Clark G. Gilbert speak to Ensign College students about holding to truth while loving people who disagree. Bring back one principle for belonging and one tension a slogan can't solve.
entries.source: Ensign College devotional, May 2022 — watch about 30 minutes.

entries.title: Racism and Other Challenges
entries.hook: What does the gospel ask of us on race and unity?
entries.blurb: President Dallin H. Oaks's BYU devotional on racism, civility, and unity. Bring back one principle for belonging and one tension a slogan can't solve.
entries.source: BYU Speeches — read the whole talk.

entries.title: Love Your Enemies
entries.hook: Can understanding an opponent make love more possible without making disagreement disappear?
entries.blurb: Arthur Brooks and Simon Sinek discuss the emotional and relational work of loving enemies. Use the conversation to think about polarization, empathy, boundaries, and the difference between understanding a person and endorsing a position.
entries.source: Arthur Brooks in conversation with Simon Sinek — watch about 30 minutes.

entries.title: Arnold Kling on the Three Languages of Politics
entries.hook: Why do people with different moral priorities talk past one another?
entries.blurb: Arnold Kling argues that progressives, conservatives, and libertarians each speak a different moral language: oppressed versus oppressor, civilization versus barbarism, freedom versus coercion. Translate one argument into a language its opponents might actually hear.
entries.source: EconTalk — listen for about 30 minutes.

entries.title: Arnold Kling on the Three Languages of Politics, Revisited
entries.hook: Has the framework held up?
entries.blurb: Kling returns years later to ask how well his three languages explain today's politics. Compare it with the original episode if you have time.
entries.source: EconTalk — listen for about 30 minutes.

entries.title: The Doctrine of Belonging
entries.hook: What does belonging require from the people who already feel at home?
entries.blurb: Elder D. Todd Christofferson teaches that belonging in the Church rests on unity, service and sacrifice, and the Atonement of Jesus Christ. Bring one concrete practice that could make a group less lonely.
entries.source: General conference, October 2022 — read the whole talk.

entries.title: One in Christ
entries.hook: What can unite people who differ in almost everything?
entries.blurb: Elder D. Todd Christofferson on finding unity in Christ across differences of culture, background, and opinion.
entries.source: General conference, April 2023 — read the whole talk.

entries.title: Come to Zion
entries.hook: What would a community of one heart and one mind look like?
entries.blurb: Elder D. Todd Christofferson describes Zion as a people of one heart and one mind, and what building it asks of each person.
entries.source: General conference, October 2008 — read the whole talk.

entries.title: By Union of Feeling We Obtain Power with God
entries.hook: What does unity make possible?
entries.blurb: Sister Sharon Eubank teaches that unity of feeling, built through small acts of understanding, gives a group real power.
entries.source: General conference, October 2020 — read the whole talk.

entries.title: Should We Get Rid of Standardized Testing?
entries.hook: What do standardized tests measure, and what do they miss?
entries.blurb: A short TED-Ed lesson on the case for and against standardized testing.
entries.source: TED-Ed — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: The Dark History of IQ Tests
entries.hook: What damage follows when a measure becomes a destiny?
entries.blurb: TED-Ed traces how IQ testing was used to justify forced sterilization and immigration limits in the early 1900s. Keep two questions apart: how tests were misused, and what they actually measure.
entries.source: TED-Ed — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: James Flynn: Why Our IQ Levels Are Higher Than Our Grandparents'
entries.hook: Why did IQ scores rise for a century?
entries.blurb: James Flynn explains the rise in IQ scores across generations and what it suggests about how minds adapt to modern life.
entries.source: TED talk — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: The Neuroscience of Intelligence: Richard Haier
entries.hook: What can brain science say about intelligence?
entries.blurb: Psychologist Richard Haier talks with Jordan Peterson about what neuroscience has learned about intelligence. Notice the difference between measuring a construct, explaining it, and deciding what a person can become.
entries.source: Jordan B. Peterson Podcast — watch or listen for about 30 minutes.

entries.title: Intelligence: An Overview of the Theories
entries.hook: How many ways can we describe human ability before the descriptions stop helping?
entries.blurb: A short Khan Academy overview of how psychologists define intelligence and the main theories they use.
entries.source: Khan Academy — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: Howard Gardner on Multiple Intelligences
entries.hook: Is there more than one kind of smart?
entries.blurb: Howard Gardner explains his theory of multiple intelligences. It is popular with teachers, and its research support is much weaker. Ask why it caught on anyway.
entries.source: Edutopia — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: Fluid and Crystallized Intelligence
entries.hook: Is the intelligence you reason with different from what you know?
entries.blurb: A short explainer on fluid intelligence (solving new problems) and crystallized intelligence (using what you've learned), and how each changes with age.
entries.source: Sprouts — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: What Is Transfer?
entries.hook: Why doesn't learning always carry over?
entries.blurb: Elon University's Center for Engaged Learning explains transfer: using what you learned in one setting somewhere new.
entries.source: Short video — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: The Quest for the Selfless Life
entries.hook: What kind of life becomes larger when it is not organized around the self?
entries.blurb: An essay by Benjamin Pacini (your instructor). Read with formation in mind: what habits make a person more attentive to God, other people, and the world in front of them?
entries.source: Benjamin Pacini on Substack — read the whole essay.

entries.title: How Will They Know?
entries.hook: How do children learn what we really believe?
entries.blurb: A short Primary song about showing love through the way we live. It takes two minutes, so pair it with something longer.
entries.source: Children's Songbook — listen to the whole song.

entries.title: I Think the World Is Glorious
entries.hook: What does gratitude for the world sound like?
entries.blurb: A short Primary song of wonder and gratitude for the world around us. It takes two minutes, so pair it with something longer.
entries.source: Children's Songbook — listen to the whole song.

entries.title: Why Your Brain Defaults to Scarcity, and How to Be Happy
entries.hook: Why does the mind fixate on what's missing?
entries.blurb: Therapy in a Nutshell explains negativity bias and the scarcity mindset, and offers practices for noticing what is good.
entries.source: Therapy in a Nutshell — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: Arthur Brooks: The Art and Science of Happiness
entries.hook: Is happiness something we feel, something we practice, or something we become?
entries.blurb: Arthur Brooks on what research says about lasting happiness and the habits that build it.
entries.source: TEDxKC — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: Daily Habits of Happy People
entries.hook: What do happy people do every day?
entries.blurb: Practical, research-informed daily habits for well-being. Notice where the speakers agree, where they differ, and where a useful practice could become an oversimplified promise.
entries.source: Therapy in a Nutshell — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: The Dedication of a Lifetime
entries.hook: What is a life worth dedicating to?
entries.blurb: President Oaks offers a demanding account of purpose, commitment, work, and discipleship. Read it as a companion to the psychological literature on well-being and ask what science can describe about a good life without deciding what a good life is for.
entries.source: BYU Speeches — listen or read for about 30 minutes.

entries.title: Maslow's Hierarchy
entries.hook: What do people need before they can flourish, and what does flourishing require beyond need satisfaction?
entries.blurb: Use Maslow's hierarchy as a historical and practical model, not a ladder that every person must climb in exactly the same order. Bring back one part that helps you think and one part that needs qualification.
entries.source: SciShow Psych — watch the whole thing.

entries.title: Peter Gray Responds to Jonathan Haidt
entries.hook: How should we respond when two thoughtful people explain the same social problem differently?
entries.blurb: Peter Gray's response to Jonathan Haidt gives you a final chance to practice charitable disagreement. Compare their accounts of childhood, play, technology, and freedom, and identify which claims are empirical, which are interpretive, and which are ultimately about values.
entries.source: Peter Gray on Substack — read for about 20 minutes.
